packet.prompt: Read only the supplied images. No web, search, repository context, catalogue, or other readings. Do not infer an identity from familiarity. These are manuscript fragments on bindings; distinguish host text and labels from the fragment. First report orientation, staves, clefs, and surviving musical runs. For each usable run give the image and approximate location, then note positions as integers in diatonic staff steps relative to the first note (0), preserving adjacent repeats. Prefer 6-14 or more consecutive notes where legible; describe uncertainty and stop at a gap or hidden span. Say which marks might be custos rather than sung notes. Report visible clef shape and line if secure; do not guess absolute pitch. Give a short literal reading of any accompanying words, with uncertainty, without completing from memory. If possible record two separate passages for later comparison. If no reliable continuous run of at least four notes remains after repeated pitches collapse, explain the visible limitation. A difficult image is not automatically unreadable: inspect the actual crops. Do not write readings of an image you could not view. Finish with coverage and limitations. Save the entire response as response.txt in this packet directory. Do not modify prompt, images, or packet.json.

text:
Image-only reading of packet 07

Orientation and surviving material

I viewed all eight supplied JPG images. Image-001 is the whole binding, with a narrow exposed manuscript strip running vertically down the central spine and small triangular exposures at four corners. The music in the spine strip is upright as photographed: each staff runs horizontally left to right, but almost all of its width is concealed by the covering. The long vertical series of visible staves must not be read as one musical sequence. The red speckled covering, the large pasted paper label, and the blue stamps are binding/ownership material, not the musical text.

Images-002, -003, and -004 enlarge consecutive regions of the central strip. They show square notation on red staves that appear to have FIVE lines where all the rules survive. Several brown shapes at the left boundary recur in the position of a clef. Some resemble a two-lobed C-type sign, particularly the pair of lobes around the second line down in the first staff below the large A in image-003. This is only a possible clef identification: wear and the fold make its outline uncertain. I do not assign absolute pitches. The conspicuous large red A and the lower red initial are letters, not clefs.

Images-005 through -008 show corner exposures, each at an oblique angle. Their rules need to be imagined horizontal before comparing vertical positions. They expose isolated noteheads or fragments of groups; they do not supply substantial consecutive runs.

Candidate passage 1: image-003, beneath the large red A, approximately x325–410, y425–690

This is the most useful musical exposure. There are two vertically paired square-note groups, one near x335 and one near x393. Each pair seems joined vertically. Four noteheads are visible, but their musical order and exact line/space placement are not fully secure.

The local red lines are approximately y430, 493, 555, 618, 682, with bending across the fold. The left pair has an upper head near the second line from the bottom and a lower head in the space below it. The right pair has an upper head near the middle line and a lower head in the space below that. This suggests two ascending two-note groups (lower head first in each pair). With that interpretation, the consecutive relative diatonic positions are:

    0, +1, +2, +3

Confidence: low to moderate for this four-note candidate, not a secure melodic fingerprint. The lower-first ordering is an interpretation of the vertically joined shapes, and the head centres are not cleanly registered against the rules. Allow approximately one staff step of uncertainty at the worn/folded locations. If the pairs instead read upper-first, their positional sequence would be approximately:

    0, -1, +2, +1

That alternative is given to make the ordering uncertainty explicit, not as another independent passage. The first interpretation seems more plausible from the near-vertical stacking. I stop before the right covering edge: another small mark at that edge is too incomplete to add. The four central heads look more like sung notes than custos marks. There is insufficient exposed staff width to establish the true line ending.

The black text just below looks approximately “fac…”; the last character is cut by the covering. This is a literal tentative reading, not a completion of a word.

Candidate passage 2: image-003, lower staff, approximately x325–430, y1220–1460

A further vertically paired group occurs near x339, followed to its right by a square head near x417. The pair's lower head lies roughly in the space above the second line from the top of the lower part of this staff, while its upper head lies near the line immediately above; the rightmost head lies approximately one staff step below the pair's lower head. Using the same provisional lower-first reading:

    0, +1, -1

This is only three candidate notes; exact placement of the upper head could shift by one step. If the pair reads upper-first instead, the approximate sequence is 0, -1, -2. I cannot extend either sequence through the covering. The rightmost square is close to the cut boundary and could theoretically be a custos, although no distinctive custos form is secure. It must not be automatically included as a sung note in a melody search.

Other central-strip exposures

Image-002: three small musical portions are visible between text rows. In the upper portion there is one clear square near x380, with worn clef-like shapes to its left. In the middle portion there is a square around x369 and a higher square at the covering edge around x442; their approximate relative positions, if both are sung notes, are 0, +1. There is only one clear square in the lowest portion, around x404. The brown, rounded shapes along the left edge should not be converted into a string of notes; several are more plausibly clef parts or damaged marks. Literal text fragments include approximately “ien…” (uncertain), “dan…” (uncertain), “san…”, and “qu…”. None licenses a completed word.

Image-003: between the two passages described above is a short exposure around y835–1095 containing two separate squares near x339 and x391. Their levels appear close, with the right one possibly one diatonic step lower: 0, -1? This is too short and too affected by the fold to use as an independent identifying run. The nearby text is only partly visible; I can distinguish roughly “…ir…” or “…ur…”, not a confident word.

Image-004: the upper surviving music includes one square near x330 and portions of marks at the right covering edge. A middle staff has one square around x347. The bottom staff, partly occupied by the red initial, exposes two adjacent dark shapes at the covering edge but not a reliably ordered run. Black text fragments look approximately “se …”, “ip…” and “om…”, each uncertain or incomplete. The small red word above the bottom initial is not securely legible; I would not normalize it into a rubric name.

Corner exposures

Image-005: oblique rules with one clear dark square near the upper corner, an adjacent elongated brown mark, and another isolated square far lower left on a different exposed strip of staff. No four-note continuous sequence. The single black letter-like shape below the upper notes is not a securely readable word.

Image-006: an oblique text fragment is visibly “…nus” or “…mus” (first letter uncertain). A single square is exposed at the lower tip of the triangle, with another partial dark shape near the top boundary. Their intervening span is hidden; they are not consecutive notes.

Image-007: only a small isolated dark mark at the lower-left staff exposure and a cropped black word fragment. The letters resemble “d…”, followed by minims, but I cannot securely transcribe the word. The mark could be part of a note or a boundary sign; there is no musical run.

Image-008: one clear square and a paler lower mark, possibly forming a two-note group, occur near the upper-right exposed triangle. Their order and completeness are uncertain. The black words below read “et u…” or “et n…”; “et” is the secure part. Another pale mark near the lower-left paper boundary is separated by concealed material and should not be joined to the upper pair.

Coverage and limitations

All eight images were actually inspected. The central strip supplies a plausible four-note candidate, but no reliable continuous run of six or more notes. The four-note candidate remains contingent on the ordering and staff registration of two vertical groups; I would not call it a secure continuous run of at least four notes after repeated pitches collapse. There is no securely readable long run that can be recovered simply by joining the isolated notes from successive staves or corner patches. The principal limitation is physical concealment of almost the entire horizontal extent of each staff, compounded by the spine fold and abrasion. No identity, absolute pitch, or missing text has been inferred.
